name: Times Literary Supplement cryptic crossword No 1,164

solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing; the grid proves the blog's enumeration wrong at 3 down, recounted from the answer here

clue.text: Starting point for translating Welsh novel

indicators.note: translating turns words into another form, so these letters are carried over into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written, all thirteen letters

explanation.surface: A reader hunts for a good place to begin translating some novel written in Welsh.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Welsh' looks like the language, but it is Irvine Welsh, the Scottish author of TRAINSPOTTING (1993).
explanation.definitionFit: Irvine Welsh wrote this Edinburgh drug-culture novel, so it is a book by the writer called Welsh.

clue.text: Hegel put off tackling a philosopher’s novel

indicators.note: something gone off has spoiled and lost its proper form, so these letters are disordered
to tackle is to grab hold of something, so the jumble wraps itself around a letter

explanation.surface: The philosopher Hegel postpones getting to grips with some thinker's novel.
explanation.walkthrough: The rearranged HEGEL PUT takes in A to give THE PLAGUE; Hegel is only fodder, and the philosopher in the definition is Albert Camus.
explanation.definitionFit: Albert Camus, the existentialist thinker, wrote La Peste, known in English under this title, about an epidemic in Oran.

clue.text: Ms. Bowles hasn’t the head to collaborate

indicators.note: lacking a head means the first letter has been taken away

blocks.note: Sally Bowles is the cabaret singer in Isherwood's Goodbye to Berlin

explanation.surface: A woman named Bowles lacks the mind to work alongside others.
explanation.walkthrough: Ms. Bowles is Sally Bowles from Christopher Isherwood's Berlin stories, later the heroine of Cabaret; drop her S.
explanation.definitionFit: As a verb, to join forces or unite with someone for a shared aim is to work together or cooperate.

clue.text: Drunk hens down about posh Bridget’s job

definitions.note: the definition names a job; the answer is the person doing it

indicators.note: a drunk staggers about out of order, so these letters lurch into a new arrangement
about means around, so the jumble goes round a single letter

blocks.note: U means upper-class, as in U and non-U speech

explanation.surface: Tipsy women at a hen party knock back drinks around the posh Bridget at work.
explanation.walkthrough: Bridget is Bridget Jones, Helen Fielding's heroine, who works as a television reporter; a hen party is a British bride's night out before her wedding.
explanation.definitionFit: Bridget Jones becomes a TV news reporter, and an eager journalist chasing stories is informally called this.

clue.text: Logger in high spirits by hollowed out yews

indicators.note: hollowing scoops out the inside, leaving only the outer shell of the word

blocks.note: first and last letters of the trees

explanation.surface: A lumberjack is in a cheerful mood beside some gutted yew trees.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Logger' suggests a lumberjack among the yews, but here it is someone who keeps a log: Samuel PEPYS, the seventeenth-century diarist.
explanation.definitionFit: Samuel Pepys kept a famous daily diary of 1660s London, so he recorded events like a ship's log keeper.

clue.text: Play about politician’s set teeth on edge!

indicators.note: being on edge means agitated and unsettled, so these letters are jumbled up
about means around, so the jumble is placed round another piece

explanation.surface: A drama about some politician is so grating it sets the audience's teeth on edge.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Set teeth on edge' reads as one idiom, but it splits: SET TEETH is the fodder and 'on edge' the signal; the 's is just 'has'.
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare's late romance about Prospero and his island storm is among his best-known stage works.

clue.text: Paper and books opened by one Prince Myshkin?

indicators.note: a thing opened by something has that something placed at its front

explanation.surface: A newspaper and a stack of books are handed over by one Russian prince.
explanation.walkthrough: ID is short for identity papers; OT, the Old Testament, is a standard crossword 'books'. The question mark marks the definition by example.
explanation.definitionFit: Prince Myshkin is the hero of Dostoevsky's novel The Idiot, called so for his naive goodness.

clue.text: Doctor’s up in anger about chap who continued Fleming’s work

indicators.note: in a down entry, going up means the letters are read from bottom to top
about can mean round and about, so these letters are moved around
in says one piece sits inside another

explanation.surface: A doctor gets worked up and furious over the man who carried on Fleming's research.
explanation.walkthrough: Fleming suggests Alexander Fleming and penicillin, beside a doctor; it is Ian Fleming, whose James Bond novels John GARDNER continued.
explanation.definitionFit: John Gardner wrote over a dozen official James Bond continuation novels after Ian Fleming's death.

clue.text: Vacuous imbeciles back king and country

indicators.note: something vacuous is empty, so only the outside letters remain
going back means reading the letters in the opposite direction

explanation.surface: Empty-headed fools support their monarch and nation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Back' reads as supporting the king, as fools might; it actually turns LEAR round. Lear is the default literary king in crosswords.
explanation.definitionFit: The Middle Eastern state on the Mediterranean is a nation, so it fits the plain word for a sovereign land.

clue.text: Copperfield’s boss is mostly exhausted and down

indicators.note: mostly means not quite all, so the final letter is cut off

explanation.surface: David Copperfield's employer is worn out and depressed.
explanation.walkthrough: In Dickens's David Copperfield, Mr SPENLOW is the proctor to whom David is articled, and the father of Dora, whom David marries.
explanation.definitionFit: David trains as a proctor under Mr Spenlow of Spenlow and Jorkins, so he is the young man's employer.

clue.text: Soldiers mass in support for Urquhart’s position?

indicators.note: in places one group inside another

blocks.note: a pier is a supporting pillar

explanation.surface: Troops gather to back someone named Urquhart in his post.
explanation.walkthrough: Francis Urquhart is the scheming Prime Minister in Michael Dobbs's House of Cards; RE, the Royal Engineers, is a British army corps.
explanation.definitionFit: Urquhart schemes his way to become Prime Minister, and the head of a government is also called this.

clue.text: Moral story that doesn’t start well enough?

indicators.note: a word that never starts has lost its opening letter

blocks.note: a fable is a short tale with a moral

explanation.surface: A cautionary tale that never gets going is barely adequate.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags a loose definition: someone well enough to do something is fit or capable.
explanation.definitionFit: Being fit or sufficiently healthy to manage a task means having the capacity to do it.

clue.text: Bust weight enthrals The Queen’s biographer (amongst other things)

indicators.note: to enthral is to hold captive, so one piece holds another

explanation.surface: A broken scale holds the biographer of Queen Elizabeth spellbound.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The Queen's biographer' reads as a royal life story; Queen is just ER, slipped between the bust and the weight, and the 's means 'is'. G.K. CHESTERTON wrote lives of Dickens, Browning and St Francis.
explanation.definitionFit: G.K. Chesterton, best known for Father Brown, also wrote studies of Dickens, Chaucer and Aquinas, among much else.

clue.text: Still something found in a writer’s bureau, I’m told?

indicators.note: what a person is told reaches them by ear, so the spoken sound is what counts

blocks.clueFragment: something found in a writer’s bureau
blocks.note: paper, envelopes and pens kept in a desk

explanation.surface: Something lies motionless in a writer's desk, or so the speaker hears.
explanation.walkthrough: The writing materials and the word for motionless differ only in one vowel and are said the same; a bureau here is a writing desk.
explanation.definitionFit: Still as an adjective means not moving, which is exactly the sense of standing fixed in place.

clue.text: “I can’t stand a naked _ _, anymore than I can a rude remark or a vulgar action ” (Tennessee Williams)

definitions.text: “I can’t stand a naked _ _, anymore than I can a rude remark or a vulgar action ”

blocks.clueFragment: “I can’t stand a naked _ _, anymore than I can a rude remark or a vulgar action ”
blocks.note: a sentence with a two-word gap for a household item that can be bare or shaded
the source is A Streetcar Named Desire, spoken by Blanche DuBois

explanation.walkthrough: This is a quotation clue: Blanche DuBois covers the bare lamp with a paper lantern to soften the harsh light on her face.
explanation.definitionFit: A glass electric lamp without a shade is called naked, which Blanche finds as coarse as rude talk.

clue.text: McEwan’s novel bet on greyhounds brings in pound

indicators.note: bringing something in takes it inside, so one piece is placed within another

blocks.note: to back is to bet on, and greyhounds are dogs
L for libra, the pound sterling

explanation.surface: A punter's wager on dog racing brings in a quid.
explanation.walkthrough: Ian McEwan's 1992 novel BLACK DOGS takes its title from Churchill's name for depression; a quid is British slang for a pound.
explanation.definitionFit: Ian McEwan published this short novel in 1992, about a couple haunted by an encounter with two fierce animals.

clue.text: Publicity about champion horse bred for its gait

indicators.note: about means around, so one piece goes round the other

blocks.note: an ace is a top performer

explanation.surface: Press attention surrounds a prize-winning horse bred for its stride.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Champion horse' looks like one phrase, but the horse belongs to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Pacers are harness-racing horses whose distinctive lateral two-beat stride moves both legs on one side together.

clue.text: Type of drama to see upcoming Othello?

indicators.note: in a down entry, coming up means the letters run from bottom to top

blocks.note: to see someone is to date or woo them
Othello is the Moor of Venice

explanation.surface: A theatregoer asks what kind of play the forthcoming Othello is.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Upcoming' suggests a new production, but it turns the Moor upside down in this down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: A courtroom drama is a genre of plays and films built around a trial, such as Twelve Angry Men.

clue.text: Sort of literary type to get on with books

blocks.note: to get on is to grow older

explanation.surface: A bookish person is advised to get on with reading.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Get on with books' sounds like advice to a reader; 'get on' means grow old, and NT, the New Testament, is a standard crossword 'books'.
explanation.definitionFit: A literary agent represents authors to publishers, so the word is completed by the adjective in the definition.

clue.text: A Liberal Democrat and wealthy bad boy author?

explanation.surface: A rich Lib Dem politician turns out to be a writer with a wild reputation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bad boy author' suggests a notorious writer, but it points to Thomas Bailey ALDRICH's The Story of a Bad Boy (1870).
explanation.definitionFit: Thomas Bailey Aldrich wrote The Story of a Bad Boy, a semi-autobiographical New England boyhood novel.

clue.text: US deals do badly, work of a Russian?

indicators.note: doing something badly means botching it, so these letters come out in the wrong order

explanation.surface: American trade agreements fare poorly, perhaps the doing of a Russian.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests political meddling; the Russian is Nikolai Gogol, whose 1842 novel concerns buying dead serfs.
explanation.definitionFit: Gogol's satirical novel about a swindler purchasing deceased serfs is a classic book by a Russian writer.

clue.text: They’ll have one on the rocks with their Lilt

definitions.text: They’ll have one on the rocks with their Lilt

blocks.clueFragment: They’ll have one on the rocks with their Lilt
blocks.note: surface reading: drinkers ordering spirits over ice with a can of the fruit soda Lilt

blocks.clueFragment: one on the rocks with their Lilt
blocks.note: setter's reading: singers whose lilting song wrecks a sailor on the rocks

explanation.surface: Bar customers order their drink over ice with a tropical soda.
explanation.walkthrough: Lilt is a British pineapple-and-grapefruit soft drink, so 'on the rocks' reads as ice; really it is shipwreck, and a lilt is a tune.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek myth these sea nymphs lured sailors with enchanting song until their ships struck the rocks.

clue.text: Dyke gets angry with so-so TV writer

indicators.note: someone who gets angry is stirred up, so these letters are thrown into disorder

explanation.surface: Greg Dyke loses his temper with a mediocre television scriptwriter.
explanation.walkthrough: Greg Dyke was a BBC director-general, which makes the TV writer seem his target; 'with' joins two lots of letters that are scrambled together.
explanation.definitionFit: Fyodor Dostoevsky, author of Crime and Punishment, is one of the great Russian novelists.

clue.text: “If there are no spots on a — cube then I’ve just put dice in my tea” (Robert Rankin)

definitions.text: “If there are no spots on a — cube then I’ve just put dice in my tea”

blocks.clueFragment: “If there are no spots on a — cube then I’ve just put dice in my tea”
blocks.note: a sentence with a gap for something sweet that comes in small cubes
the source is the British comic fantasy novelist

explanation.walkthrough: This is a quotation clue: the joke is that a lump for sweetening tea and a die are both small cubes, told apart only by the spots.
explanation.definitionFit: Sweetener sold in compressed lumps is dropped into a hot drink, unlike dice, which carry pips.

clue.text: French wine overwhelms edith Nesbit initially – it’s toxic stuff

indicators.note: initially means at the start, so each word gives its opening letter
to overwhelm is to engulf, so one piece swallows another

explanation.surface: A French wine floors the children's author Edith Nesbit, being poisonous.
explanation.walkthrough: E. Nesbit wrote The Railway Children; VENIN is the poisonous substance in snake venom.
explanation.definitionFit: Venin is a chemistry term for any of the poisonous compounds found in animal venoms.

clue.text: Lead the FBI’s Clarice half dismissed

indicators.note: dismissing half sends away half the letters, leaving the rest

blocks.note: Clarice Starling, the FBI trainee in The Silence of the Lambs

explanation.surface: The FBI agent Clarice heads an investigation, only to be half sacked.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lead' looks like a verb about leading the FBI, but it is the noun for a principal role; Clarice Starling is Thomas Harris's heroine.
explanation.definitionFit: The lead in a film or play is the principal performer, the top-billed name on the poster.

clue.text: Name for rabbit about to be potted by British queen

indicators.note: potting a thing puts it inside a pot, so one piece is held by another

explanation.surface: A rabbit's name is about to be shot by a British queen.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Potted' suggests shooting a rabbit for the pot; it means put inside. Brer Rabbit is the trickster of the Uncle Remus tales.
explanation.definitionFit: Brer, dialect for brother, is the title before the animals' names in Joel Chandler Harris's stories.

clue.text: Yarn that’s a part of Chasing Rainbows

indicators.note: a part of a phrase is a stretch of it, so the letters lie inside the words

explanation.surface: A tale that forms one strand of a story called Chasing Rainbows.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Yarn' wants to be a story; it is thread dyed before weaving.
explanation.definitionFit: Ingrain yarn is dyed in the fibre before spinning, so the term names a type of woollen thread.

clue.text: Play 45 minutes then change ends for Northern FA

indicators.note: changing ends swaps the first and last places, as teams do at half-time

blocks.note: three quarters of the word for sixty minutes
nowt is northern English for nothing, as is sweet FA

explanation.surface: A footballer plays one half, then the sides switch ends for a northern league.
explanation.walkthrough: Forty-five minutes is three quarters of an HOUR, so lose a quarter of its letters. FA is not the Football Association but Fanny Adams, as in sweet FA, British slang for nothing.
explanation.definitionFit: Thornton Wilder's 1938 drama about the small town of Grover's Corners is a celebrated American stage work.

clue.text: Rabbit, badger and nag weathered bad storm

indicators.note: something weathered has been worn and reshaped by the elements, so these letters are altered
bad means faulty, so these letters are in the wrong order

blocks.note: to badger or harry is to pester

explanation.surface: A rabbit, a badger and an old horse ride out a fierce storm together.
explanation.walkthrough: The animals suggest a country tale, but Rabbit is the nickname of John Updike's hero HARRY ANGSTROM in the Rabbit novels.
explanation.definitionFit: Updike's four Rabbit novels follow Harry 'Rabbit' Angstrom, a former basketball star, through middle America.
